summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — establishes national commission and reporting requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

regulations_applicable.title: Agency 30 - KANSAS DEPARTMENT FOR CHILDREN AND FAMILIES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Estate of B.I.C. ex rel. C.S.C. v. Gillen
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case arising from the death of a Kansas toddler, the court reversed summary judgment for a Kansas SRS social worker on the state-created danger claim, holding that genuine issues of material fact precluded qualified immunity, while affirming summary judgment on the familial association claims.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Kansas-origin federal case on liability after a child dies following agency contact, and it identifies the affirmative acts that can support a claim.
key_cases.quote: We agree that qualified immunity was not appropriate on the state danger-creation claim given genuine issues of material fact

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that foster care is a custodial relationship giving rise to a special relationship between the State and the child, which creates a continuing constitutional duty to protect that is violated when officials know of a danger or fail to exercise professional judgment.
key_cases.relevance: The death or serious injury of a child in foster care is actionable under the special relationship doctrine in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: foster care is recognized as one of the custodial relationships that creates a special relationship

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to a caseworker who recommended and facilitated a child's placement with an abusive father while withholding known adverse information, holding that on the facts viewed in the child's favor she violated his clearly established substantive due process right to be free from state-created danger.
key_cases.relevance: Serious injury to a child following a caseworker's affirmative placement recommendation supports a substantive due process claim in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that, under Currier, Ms. Patton violated T.D.'s clearly established substantive due process constitutional right to be free of a state official's creation of danger from a private actor

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed judgment for the county, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence merely because caseworkers knew of the danger, while noting that a custodial relationship such as state-operated foster care might be different.
key_cases.relevance: A child's death at a parent's hands after agency contact does not, without more, establish a federal due process violation.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for SRS workers sued for a negligent child abuse investigation preceding a child's death, holding that the reporting and investigation statute creates only a duty to the public at large and that the decision whether to open a file for further investigation is a discretionary function immune under the Kansas Tort Claims Act.
key_cases.relevance: The case arose from a child's death after SRS declined to open a file, and it forecloses tort recovery on those facts.
key_cases.quote: The decision whether to open a file for further investigation is a discretionary function

key_cases.case_name: C.J.W. ex rel. L.W. v. State
key_cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for the State in a suit by a 12-year-old assaulted in juvenile detention, holding that the State owed him a duty under Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 315, 319 and 320 to warn of and protect against a known dangerous detainee, that the discretionary function exception did not immunize breach of that legally imposed duty, and that controverted facts precluded summary judgment.
key_cases.relevance: A child seriously harmed while in state custody has a Kansas tort claim where the State knew of the danger, notwithstanding the Tort Claims Act.
key_cases.quote: Children who are taken into custody should be protected from others in custody
